summary: Duolingo has been a fun and engaging tool for Sofia to reconnect with her heritage language, providing a great balance between learning and entertainment.
top_quotes: You know, Duolingo makes learning Spanish feel like a game instead of a chore, which is amazing for staying consistent!
Las notificaciones de Duolingo son un poco como mi abuelita diciéndome, '¡No te olvides de practicar!'
Honestly, being able to improve my Spanish while just sitting on my couch for five minutes is a game-changer.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey there! I'm Sofia, super excited to chat with you today. Let's dive in!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Sure! So, I was born and raised in Texas to Mexican parents. Grew up speaking Spanglish at home, you know, mezcla de inglés y español. I always wanted to work in healthcare, so I became a nurse. Love helping people and making a difference. Now, I'm focusing on improving my formal Spanish, especially for my job. It's been quite a journey!

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in a small town in Texas, not far from San Antonio. It's one of those places where everybody knows each other, and there's a real sense of community.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: It was warm and friendly, you know? Lots of family gatherings, plenty of good food, and a mix of cultures. I mean, even in school, it felt like one big family. There were challenges too, but overall, it was a great place to be a kid.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: A big turning point was definitely when I decided to go into nursing. I remember volunteering at a local clinic during high school and realizing how much I enjoyed helping people. That's when it clicked for me that I wanted to make a career out of it.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, it changed everything. Before that, I wasn't sure what I wanted to do. Going into nursing gave me a sense of direction and purpose. It also opened up so many opportunities, like meeting amazing people and learning about different cultures.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I just went for it, to be honest. I researched nursing programs, talked to mentors, and applied to nursing school. It was challenging at times, with lots of late-night studying, but I stayed focused on my goal and pushed through.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it's all about balancing my work as a nurse and continuing to improve my Spanish. It's important for me to connect with patients on a deeper level, especially those who are more comfortable speaking Spanish. Plus, it's a personal journey to connect with my heritage.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Because language is such a powerful tool for connection. It's not just about the words but the cultural context behind them. Being able to communicate effectively with Spanish-speaking patients means I can provide better care and build trust.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day starts with a peaceful morning coffee, followed by a productive day at work. If I get to have meaningful interactions with patients and maybe learn something new, that's a win. Ending the day with some Duolingo practice and a relaxing evening at home is just perfect.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: When I've done something that feels meaningful, like helping a patient or learning a new Spanish phrase. Also, when there's time for a little fun and laughter, either with coworkers or at home with my family.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I try to weigh the pros and cons first, but I also trust my gut a lot. Talking things over with my family or friends helps too, because they often have insights I might not consider. It's like getting different perspectives before deciding.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Um, I'd say I'm a mix. I like to have a plan, especially for work-related things, but I'm also flexible. Life rarely goes exactly as planned, so you gotta be ready to adapt.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, just last month we had a big family gathering, and I had planned to make enchiladas. Last minute, we found out there were more people coming, so I had to quickly adjust, adding a few extra dishes. It turned out great, though, because everyone pitched in to help.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I'm pretty cautious by nature, especially when it comes to big risks. I try to do my research and think things through. But sometimes, you just have to take a leap of faith if it feels right. You know, estar en la zona de confort no siempre es bueno.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday starts with a quick breakfast and some coffee. I head off to work, where my day could include anything from routine check-ups to emergency situations. After work, I try to squeeze in a quick Duolingo session before preparing dinner. Evenings are often spent either relaxing with my family or catching up with friends over the phone.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely work. As a nurse, you always have to be on your toes, both physically and emotionally. It's rewarding, but it can be draining. So I really value my downtime when I can just recharge.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time for hobbies, like maybe taking a cooking class or just exploring new places. I'd also love to dedicate more time to improve my Spanish beyond just the basics, like getting into some literature.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Last year, it was definitely time. With the pandemic, work was more demanding than ever, and I had less time for myself or personal projects. It was all about adapting to changes and ensuring I could support my patients as best as possible.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: By focusing on what I can control and trying to stay organized. I also had to learn to prioritize self-care, like making sure I get enough rest and finding small ways to relax throughout the day. Little things add up, you know?

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I'd say my family and a few close friends. My sister and I are especially close, and I always know I can count on her. My parents are also a big part of my life, and I'm really grateful for our relationship.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: With my family, it's a lot of love and laughter. We're supportive of each other, and even when we disagree, we always find a way to come together. My friends are like my chosen family, always there to uplift and challenge me when needed.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, at work and at home. Those are my main hubs. Work is where I spend most of my day, and home is where I relax and recharge.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Work can be intense, but it's fulfilling. I feel a sense of purpose there. At home, it's a blend of comfort and peace. It's my safe haven where I can just be myself and unwind after a long day.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: At work, it's the satisfaction of helping people and making a difference. At home, it's the familiar routines, the warmth of family, and the little things, like cooking a meal or just kicking back on the couch.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Definitely my sister and my close friends. They know me well and always give me honest advice. Talking it out with them helps me see things from different angles, which often makes the problem feel more manageable.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: Losing a patient to COVID-19 was incredibly tough. It hit me hard because you build connections, and despite doing everything you can, sometimes it isn't enough. It was a real reminder of how fragile life can be.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It made me feel helpless at first. But it also reinforced why I'm in this profession. It drove home the importance of showing up every day and doing my best, no matter how difficult things get.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I talked to colleagues who were going through similar feelings. We leaned on each other and shared stories. I also turned to my family for support, and practiced mindfulness, you know, just to keep focus and stay grounded.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, a bit of everything: música, meditation, and sometimes just a good cry, you know? Talking with loved ones is a huge relief, and doing something creative or physical, like cooking or yoga, also helps.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I'd love to be more fluent in Spanish, maybe even teaching others. Career-wise, I'd want to continue making an impact in healthcare, maybe moving into a leadership role to influence positive changes. Personal life? Hopefully travel more, spend time with family, and just enjoy the little moments.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: More balance in my life, for sure. I'd like less stress and more time to pursue my hobbies and interests. Maybe a little more travel and adventure, too. And definitely being even more fluent in Spanish!

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I mostly relied on speaking with family and friends, which is great for conversational Spanish, but I lacked the formal structure. I tried using textbooks and some online resources, but it was difficult to stay consistent and motivated.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the lack of engagement and consistency. I would start off strong, but the materials I used felt dry and not very interactive, so I'd lose interest quickly. Plus, it was hard to track progress without some sort of feedback.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when I was preparing for a trip to Mexico, and I realized I wasn't retaining as much as I thought. Speaking with locals was challenging, and I felt like all those hours of study didn't really pay off in real-world scenarios.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A friend recommended it to me a couple of years ago. She said it was fun and easy to use, and since it's an app, I could practice anywhere, which sounded perfect for my schedule.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, the convenience was a big factor. The idea that I could just pull out my phone and practice wherever, whenever was super appealing. Plus, it was free, so it felt like there was nothing to lose by giving it a shot.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Okay, so the other day, I was sitting in the break room at work. I pulled out my phone and opened up Duolingo. I got this fun notification that reminded me I've kept my streak going. I jumped into a lesson on formal greetings. It had me matching phrases and repeating sentences aloud. I love the quick quizzes at the end that let me know how I'm doing. It's like a little game break during the day, you know?

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The ability to repeat and review is super helpful. I love that if I mess up, I get the chance to do it again and really understand why my answer was wrong. Plus, it's nice to have the audio to practice pronunciation, which is something I struggled with before.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, the repetitive nature of certain exercises can get a bit tedious. And there are moments when I wish there was a little more explanation around grammar rules. You know, like a brief side note on why something is the way it is, más contexto.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: I think it's when I feel like I've outgrown certain lessons but can't skip ahead without going through all of them. It can feel a bit limiting when I want to challenge myself more but I'm stuck going over basics I've mastered.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Ah, just last week I was trying to level up, and I had to repeat some exercises I already knew well. It was a bit frustrating because I felt ready to move on, but the app insisted I review. It seemed like a waste of time, pero ni modo, you gotta trust the process sometimes.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, occasionally. I sometimes use other resources like YouTube or language podcasts for more context and explanations. It's nice to have different angles, especially for more complex grammar or cultural nuances that the app may not cover.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me that deeper dive into the why's and how's of the language. Sometimes I need more than just the basics, especially when it comes to understanding the cultural context behind certain phrases or idioms.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case would be investing time without seeing improvements in real-world interactions. You know, like if my speaking or comprehension doesn't actually get better despite all the time I'm putting in.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it keeps me engaged while teaching me something new and useful. I want it to be that fun little break in my day that also boosts my confidence in speaking Spanish, especially more formally.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I see it working when I catch myself using new phrases naturally in conversation or when something I learned pops up in a real-world context. It's like, oh, I know this from Duolingo! Love that feeling.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I'd add more cultural context and maybe explanations for grammar rules. Just those little insights that provide a bigger picture would be super helpful and make the lessons even more comprehensive.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I'd love to see more integration between language learning and real-world applications. More interactive media or events that help bridge the gap between learning in an app and using it in real life would be amazing.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we covered a lot! Just that, overall, I'm grateful for tools like Duolingo that make learning accessible and engaging. It's exciting to think about how technology can keep evolving in this space.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, as long as it helps make language learning better and more personalized for everyone!
